        - heading "Americans with Disabilities Act" [level=1] [ref=f9e190]
        - paragraph [ref=f9e191]:
          - paragraph [ref=f9e192]:
            - strong [ref=f9e193]: What is the ADA?
          - paragraph [ref=f9e194]: The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) of 1990 was enacted to ensure all qualified individuals with disabilities enjoy the same opportunities available to individuals without disabilities. The ADA gives civil rights protections to individuals with disabilities similar to those provided to individuals on the basis of race, color, sex, national origin, age, and religion. The ADA guarantees equal opportunity for individuals with disabilities in public accommodations, employment, transportation, state and local government services, and telecommunications. The ADA applies to state courts as providers of public programs and services.
          - paragraph [ref=f9e195]: The ADA defines an “individual with a disability” as a person who has a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits one or more major life activities, a person who has a record of such an impairment, or a person who is regarded as having such an impairment. Examples of physical impairments include speech and hearing impairments, visual impairments, epilepsy, heart disease, HIV infections/AIDS, cancer, diabetes, and mobility impairments. Examples of mental impairments include learning disabilities and psychological disorders.
          - paragraph [ref=f9e196]: The ADA is divided into five sections. Title I prohibits unreasonable discrimination against qualified individuals based on a disability in all employment activities. Under Title II, a qualified individual with a disability cannot be unreasonably discriminated against or excluded from participation in or benefits of the services, programs, or activities of state and local governments, including the judicial branch. Title III prohibits discrimination by public accommodations, that is, a private entity that owns, leases, or operates a place of public accommodations. Such a place is defined as, among other things, services by doctors, lawyers, accountants, and other professionals. Title IV relates to telecommunications, and Title V contains miscellaneous provisions.
          - paragraph [ref=f9e197]
          - paragraph [ref=f9e198]:
            - strong [ref=f9e199]: What should I do if I am a qualified individual with a disability who needs a reasonable accommodation in order to participate in the employment process within the Florida State Courts System?
          - paragraph [ref=f9e200]: If you are an individual with a disability who needs a reasonable accommodation in order to participate in the application, recruitment, and/or selection process for employment within the Florida State Courts System, and you need assistance in Escambia, Santa Rosa, Okaloosa, or Walton Counties, please contact the person listed below as far in advance as possible. Please be prepared to explain your functional limitations and suggest a reasonable accommodation that will enable you to effectively participate in the employment process.
          - paragraph

            - strong [ref=f9e202]: Allison Newton, Chief Deputy Court AdministratorM. C. Blanchard Building190 W. Governmental Center, 5th FloorPensacola, FL 32502850-595-4400
          - paragraph [ref=f9e203]
          - paragraph [ref=f9e204]: If you work for or are hired by the Florida State Courts System and find that you require a reasonable accommodation in order to perform the essential functions of your position, you should consult with your immediate supervisor.
          - paragraph [ref=f9e205]:
            - strong [ref=f9e206]: What should I do if I am a qualified individual with a disability who needs assistance in order to participate in a program or service of the Florida State Courts System?
          - paragraph [ref=f9e207]: Some physical barriers make it difficult for individuals with a disability to participate in court services, programs, or proceedings. For example, in some courthouses, witness and jury boxes may not be accessible to wheelchairs or public information counters may be too high for some individuals. In addition to architecturally renovating facilities to make them readily accessible to individuals with disabilities, other methods are available to provide program access, including relocating a service, to enable an individual with a disability to participate.
          - paragraph [ref=f9e208]: "An auxiliary aid or service is any device or aid that is designed to provide effective communication and participation for individuals with disabilities. Examples of auxiliary aids or services include:"

            - listitem [ref=f9e212]: Oral interpreters
            - listitem [ref=f9e213]: Real-time transcription services
            - listitem [ref=f9e214]: Providing materials in large print, braille, or a copy of an audio recording
            - listitem [ref=f9e215]: Reader services
          - paragraph [ref=f9e216]: "Services the Florida State Courts System is not required to provide under the ADA include:"
          - list [ref=f9e217]:
            - listitem [ref=f9e218]: Transportation to and from the courthouse
            - listitem [ref=f9e219]: Legal counsel or advice
            - listitem [ref=f9e220]: Personal devices, such as wheelchairs or hearing aids
            - listitem [ref=f9e221]: Personal services, such as medical or attendant care
            - listitem [ref=f9e222]: A modification of a policy or an auxiliary aid or service that would result in a fundamental change in the nature of the program or service, or an undue burden
          - paragraph [ref=f9e223]: "If you are an individual with a disability who needs an accommodation in order to participate in a court proceeding, please contact the ADA Coordinator or Liaison for the county in which your matter is scheduled at least seven working days of receipt of your notice to appear at the following numbers:"
          - paragraph [ref=f9e224]:
            - strong [ref=f9e225]: What remedies are available to individuals with disabilities who believe their rights under the ADA have been violated?
          - paragraph [ref=f9e226]: The Florida State Courts System has established internal grievance procedures that allow for the resolution of complaints without resorting to federal complaint procedures. All individuals have a right to pursue complaints of discrimination through the Florida State Courts System’s internal grievance system.
          - paragraph [ref=f9e227]:
            - text: The First Judicial Circuit has also adopted an internal grievance system as outlined in
            - link "Administrative Order 2025-15" [ref=f9e228] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: https://cdn.sanity.io/files/xf5z3ibd/production/66c8c7136227de06a538d4d30b6f015c6b1f51f1.pdf
            - text: ", and has designated the ADA Coordinator for the First Judicial Circuit as the responsible person. You can find the First Judicial Circuit’s"
            - link "Internal Grievance Procedure here" [ref=f9e229] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: https://cdn.sanity.io/files/xf5z3ibd/production/e0434f54c1a7d11fb3c323103a65d6ccf05cb8a9.pdf
            - text: .
          - paragraph [ref=f9e230]: The ADA recommends resolving disputes on a local level, if possible. If an individual is not successful after pursuing local remedies, they are not prohibited from later seeking relief through the United States Department of Justice or the United States Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.
          - paragraph [ref=f9e231]:
            - strong [ref=f9e232]: Accommodations for Court Proceedings in the First Judicial Circuit
          - paragraph [ref=f9e233]: The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) of 1990 prohibits discrimination on the basis of disability in state and local government services. This includes participation in court proceedings. Any individual who needs an accommodation to participate in a court proceeding should contact the appropriate ADA Coordinator or Liaison for the county in which the proceeding will be held.
